title: GPU scheduler holistic triage (nsys + CUDA Graph) — Apr 2026
body:
Summary:
This is a working triage doc for a recurring pattern we see on production tail-latency: intermittent SM underutilization spikes during sustained replay of CUDA Graphs. The goal is to consolidate traces (nsys), validate hypotheses about graph fragmentation and scheduler evictions, and propose short-term mitigations for the Dedicated fleet.

High-level hypothesis:
- Large numbers of small CUDA Graph fragments + mixed-priority streams are creating micro-phases where the scheduler serializes kernels instead of sustaining SM-wide work.
- That serialization increases per-token tail latency even when average occupancy looks OK in coarse metrics.
- GPU-side preemption or stream priority inversion (host-side) could be amplifying gaps between graph replay windows.

Where we saw it:
- Production lanes: p-dedicated-1 (g5x-like) serving small-batching decode workloads for chat endpoints.
- Repro on bench: local repro with mini-replay harness (see GH PR above) reproduces 95th spike when we enable host-side graph capture + immediate launch.

Artifacts and commands used (quick):
- nsys profile: nsys profile --backtrace=none -o session_2026-04-02 --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,cudnn --duration=30s ./replay_harness --seq 512
- nvprof not used (we need timeline details).
- CUDA Graph replay wrapper: capture per-batch fragment when max_tokens < 64 (code in PR 4123).
- Filtered timeline exported as csv and opened in timeline viewer.

Key observations from traces:
1) Fragmentation clusters: we see bursts where 4-6 tiny graph launches (each < 1ms) are separated by 0.7-1.2ms gaps with no active kernels. These gaps align with host CPU activity (scheduling, epoll wakeups).
2) Kernel packing: when kernels are tightly packed they overlap and SM utilization is ~88-92%. During the gaps utilization drops to 18-30% for ~1ms windows causing tail amplification.
3) Stream priority jitter: some graph launches come from lower-priority streams due to a helper thread sending cleanup ops; when that thread wakes it pushes high-priority work back, but scheduling lag introduces ~200-500us mis-ordering in some traces.
4) CUDA Graph capture overhead: enabling eager capture for very small microbatches adds measurable host CPU cost that correlates with fragmentation.
5) No obvious memory-bound stalls in the SM (L2 utilization steady) — the issue is scheduling/phasing rather than memory throughput.

Preliminary root-cause candidates:
- Host-side batching/connectors: the path that triggers capture sometimes blocks on a mutex for pending work, adding jitter to capture->launch latency.
- Kernel launch ordering + stream priority: using multiple streams with mixed priorities creates windows where high-throughput kernels are delayed behind light-weight kernels.
- Graph fragmentation: building many tiny graphs instead of one aggregated graph increases host transition overhead and exacerbates scheduler gaps.

Experiments run so far and results:
- Merge small fragments into an aggregated graph per-sample (single capture per request) -> 95th latency drops ~18% on bench, and nsys shows much smaller gaps. Tradeoff: higher memory footprint for longer graphs.
- Single-stream replay (force all graphs launched on same high-priority stream) -> reduced jitter but slightly increased contention observed on CPU side (worker pinned).
- Add small CPU prefetch thread to warm graph objects before actual launch -> reduced first-kernel latency but not the intra-window gaps.
- Instrumented locks with perf counters -> identified one hot mutex in the capture path (CaptureQueue::pop) with heavy tail on 5% of requests.

Questions we still have:
- Are there kernel-level preemption events visible in newer driver versions that would explain sudden SM drop? (driver 530.x vs 535.x differences)
- How much of the host-side jitter is network/epoll related vs pure mutex scheduling?
- Can persistent kernel strategies (always-on kernels that accept tokens) be reused to smooth micro-gaps without rewriting capture logic?

Short-term mitigations to try (fast):
- Increase graph aggregation threshold (from fragments < 64 tokens to < 128 tokens) to reduce number of captures per request. Reasoning: fewer releases to scheduler -> fewer gaps.
- Force critical decode work onto a dedicated high-priority stream and isolate helper threads to background priority.
- Add lightweight spin-wait for 200-400us after capture before launch (experimental) — may allow coalescing of adjacent fragments. Danger: increases average latency if overused.

Longer-term/architectural options:
- Move to persistent-kernel style for small token outputs (tokenization into pipes) to avoid frequent kernel launch overhead entirely.
- Rework capture path to be fully lock-free (use ring buffer + atomic index) to eliminate mutex tail.
- Scheduler-aware graph packing: build a simple simulator to estimate the expected SM fill for candidate graph aggregates and choose partitioning that maximizes sustained utilization.

Next steps (owners):
- Daniel: prototype lock-free capture queue (spike branch) and run nsys comparison (due 2026-04-12).
- Sofia: run fleet canary with increased aggregation threshold on two Dedicated clusters, track 99th and 95th (due 2026-04-14).
- Liu: test on driver 535.x on bench nodes to see if any driver-level preemption behavior changes timeline (due 2026-04-09).
- Aisha: consolidate traces, make a short README of how to interpret the exported csv -> timeline pipeline.

Notes for reproducing (engineering tips):
- Use the repro harness with deterministic seeds and set cpu_affinity to keep worker threads on the same core group as the GPU driver threads.
- Capture nsys for 30s windows and use the "CUDA API" lane + "Kernel" lane for best correlation between host/syscalls and kernel timeline.
- Export the timeline to csv and run the simple script in tools/timeline_coalesce.py (branch in PR) to compute gap histograms.

Observational logs (short excerpts):
- 2026-04-02 19:12:12.347 - launch fragment id=1135 latency=0.83ms gap-before=0.72ms owner-thread=worker-7
- 2026-04-02 19:12:12.849 - aggregate-launch id=1138 latency=2.1ms sustained-sm=88%
- 2026-04-02 19:12:13.024 - capture-queue-pop wait=0.0009s thread=helper-2

Open risks/concerns:
- Aggregation increases memory usage and might expose OOM in worst-case heavy prompt workloads; need safety caps.
- Spin-waits increase tail if mis-applied; must be gated by a feature flag and telemetry.
- Fleet rollout needs careful SLA communication.

Appendix (links to raw traces):
- session_2026-04-02.nsys (on internal artifact store, see linked_artifacts)
- CSV exports: /artifacts/repro/session_2026-04-02/timeline.csv

If anyone has additional traces from other clusters (especially older driver versions or different NVLink topologies), attach them here. Will update after the initial experiments finish next week.

TODO:
- [ ] Add a short perf test to quantify memory overhead of aggregation strategy.
- [ ] Build a micro-simulator for graph packing heuristic.
- [ ] Prepare canary rollout checklist and metric gating for success.

End of notes.
